newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: SUMO-SYDNEY HARBOUR SHAKES AS WRESTLERS HIT TOWN.
newsitem.headline: SUMO-SYDNEY HARBOUR SHAKES AS WRESTLERS HIT TOWN.

text.p: The shores of Sydney Harbour shook on Thursday as two Japanese sumo wrestlers stomped, tossed, grunted and slapped each other in the throat in a promotional launch for Australia's first Grand Sumo tournament.
In June, 40 Japanese sumo champions will stage a knock-out tournament in Sydney and Melbourne, which will be broadcast live back to Japan to an estimated 30 million viewers.
"This is the first major sumo tournament to be staged in Australia and will bring thousands of Japanese tourists," said New South Wales state premier Bob Carr.
Japan is Australia's main tourist market.

Toshimitsu Kitanoumi, director of the Nihon Sumo Kyokai (Japan Sumo Association), said he believed sports-mad Australians would appreciate not only the sporting prowess but also the cultural aspects of sumo.

"Grand sumo is a sport built on history and tradition spanning 1,500 years and it is our hope by introducing sumo to you it will lead to better understanding of the true spirit of Japan...," Kitanoumi said.
While Thursday's bout on the shores of Sydney Harbour was promotional, sumo champion Koyo Musashimaru, tipping the scales at 202 kg (445 pounds), was in no mood to lose.
Musashimaru, born in Hawaii but now one of the top draw cards at Tokyo's sumo centre with a record 397 wins and 168 losses, politely demonstrated various moves for the press.
But when the real thing came, Musashimaru ignored the cameras, unnerving his slightly smaller opponent with a stare which could strip paint off a wall.
Thirty seconds later, after a clash of massive, sweating flesh, Musashimaru threw Toshio Yamamoto flat on his back -- a move which shook the ground and sent photographers scurrying.
